propositions.text: George Yankson is a Ghanaian citizen who claimed refugee protection in Canada based on his sexual orientation as a gay man.
propositions.quote: George Yankson is a citizen of Ghana who claimed refugee protection in Canada on the basis of his sexual orientation as a gay man.

propositions.text: The Refugee Protection Division dismissed his claim because it did not believe he is gay.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dismissed his claim because it did not believe that he is gay.

propositions.text: The Refugee Appeal Division dismissed his appeal.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismissed his appeal.

propositions.text: He now seeks judicial review of the RAD decision.
propositions.quote: He now seeks judicial review of the RAD decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Yankson, a Ghanaian, claimed refugee protection as a gay man; RPD and RAD dismissed his claim and appeal; he seeks judicial review.

propositions.text: He has always been attracted to men but did not act due to illegality in Ghana.
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that he has always been attracted to men, but did not act on his feelings because homosexuality is forbidden and illegal in Ghana.

propositions.text: He had his first sexual experience in November 2013 at age 18.
propositions.quote: He states that he had his first sexual experience in November 2013, when he was 18 years old.

propositions.text: His first partner died in a car accident shortly after their relationship started.
propositions.quote: His partner was killed in a car accident shortly after their relationship started.

propositions.text: He began a second relationship soon after and it lasted some time.
propositions.quote: He began a relationship with another partner a short time later, and that relationship continued for some time.

propositions.text: In March 2014, he and his partner were discovered at school and he was forced to flee and leave school.
propositions.quote: In March 2014, the Applicant and his partner were discovered at school, and the Applicant was forced to flee to escape. His mother was informed of what had happened, and he was forced to leave the school.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states he was attracted to men but acted cautiously; had two relationships; was discovered at school and forced to flee and leave school.

propositions.text: He endured harassment and mistreatment due to his sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant says he endured harassment and mistreatment by people in his community because of his sexual orientation.

propositions.text: He left to visit grandmother but was ordered to leave after she discovered his partner.
propositions.quote: He eventually left to visit his grandmother in another city, but during his stay there, she discovered him with this partner, and ordered him to leave.

propositions.text: He returned to live with his mother.
propositions.quote: He returned to live with his mother.

propositions.text: His mother’s bakery lost customers and closed due to hostility related to his sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant says that his mother’s bakery business lost customers and eventually closed because people were hostile towards her because of his sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant says he faced harassment, was ordered to leave grandmother's home, returned to mother, whose bakery closed due to hostility.

propositions.text: He was attacked by a neighbour who burned his arm with a hot iron.
propositions.quote: The Applicant says he was attacked by a neighbour who burned his arm with a hot iron.

propositions.text: He decided to flee Ghana and obtained a student visa in March 2016, arriving in Canada in May 2016.
propositions.quote: He then decided that he had to flee Ghana. With the assistance of an agent, he obtained a student visa in March 2016 and arrived in Canada in early May 2016.

propositions.text: He claimed refugee protection upon arrival in Canada.
propositions.quote: He claimed refugee protection upon his arrival.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant was attacked, fled Ghana, obtained a student visa, arrived in Canada, and claimed refugee protection.

propositions.text: The RPD dismissed the claim due to lack of credibility and little weight to supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD dismissed the Applicant’s claim, finding that his testimony lacked credibility and that the supporting evidence he filed should be given very little weight.

propositions.text: RPD noted discrepancies in testimony about first relationship duration and contradictions with Basis of Claim Form.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that there were significant discrepancies in the Applicant’s testimony about how long his first relationship had lasted, and that his evidence contradicted the information in his Basis of Claim Form.

propositions.text: Applicant's inability to state full details of second partner during second port of entry interview undermined credibility.
propositions.quote: It also found that his inability to state the full name, date of birth or address of his second partner when he was questioned during his second port of entry interviewalso undermined his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD dismissed the claim due to credibility issues, discrepancies in testimony, and inability to provide partner details at second interview.

propositions.text: RPD discounted supporting evidence including letters and community participation as unsworn and unavailable for testimony.
propositions.quote: This evidence was discounted by the RPD, because it was not contained in sworn documents, the authors were not available to testify, and the information about his participation in the LGBT community in Canada did not establish his sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD discounted unsworn letters and community participation evidence due to lack of sworn status and unavailable authors.

propositions.text: RPD concluded Applicant had not established he is gay and dismissed refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD therefore concluded that the Applicant had not established that he is gay, and it dismissed his refugee claim.

propositions.text: Applicant appealed the RPD decision to the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant appealed this to the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD dismissed the claim for not establishing sexual orientation; the applicant appealed to the RAD.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed appeal, agreeing RPD did not err in concluding Applicant was never in same-sex relationship in Ghana.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismissed the appeal, finding that the RPD had not erred in concluding that the Applicant was never in a same sex relationship in Ghana.

propositions.text: Applicant's inability to give second partner's last name or date of birth at port of entry impugned credibility.
propositions.quote: It found that the Applicant’s inability to give his second partner’s last name or date of birth to the officer at the port of entry did impugn his credibility, as did the contradictions about when that relationship had ended.

propositions.text: RAD referred to SOGIE Guideline and noted discomfort with authority could affect reluctance to disclose sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The RAD referred to the Chairperson’s Guideline 9: Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (the SOGIE Guideline) and noted that discomfort with authority figures and fear of being turned away could conceivably affect a claimant’s reluctance to disclose his or her sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismissed the appeal, agreed on credibility issues, and referenced SOGIE Guideline about reluctance to disclose sexual orientation.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant explained fear of being sent back due to debts, not sexual orientation, and delayed mentioning sexual orientation until second interview end.
propositions.quote: On the facts of this case, however, the RAD concluded that the Applicant had explained in some detail his fear of being sent back to Ghana because he owed money to people and he did not have the funds to repay them. It was only at the end of his second interview that the Applicant made any reference to his sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Applicant expressed concern about inability to visit family in Ghana after refugee claim process explained.
propositions.quote: In addition, when the process of making a refugee claim was explained to him, the Applicant expressed concern that he would not be able to go back to Ghana to visit his family.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant's fear related to debts, sexual orientation mentioned late, and concern about visiting family after claim process explained.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant's belated sexual orientation statement likely due to truthfulness about initial fear, consistent with desire to repay debts and visit family.
propositions.quote: While I acknowledge that his belated statement about his sexual orientation could be due to discomfort with the officers, the more simple explanation is more credible to me: the [Applicant] was telling the truth when he was first asked about his fear. This explanation is also consistent with his desire to return to Ghana to visit his family after he had earned some money to repay his lenders, which money would not protect him if his real fear was of anti-gay violence.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Applicant's late sexual orientation disclosure more likely truthful fear explanation consistent with debt repayment and family visit desire.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant's evidence on first same-sex relationship vague and contradictory, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD also found that the Applicant’s evidence regarding his first same sex relationship was vague and contradictory, and combined with the other difficulties with his evidence, this undermined his credibility.

propositions.text: RAD rejected procedural fairness argument about RPD giving little weight to supporting documentation without notice or response opportunity.
propositions.quote: The RAD rejected the argument that the RPD had breached procedural fairness by giving little weight to the supporting documentation the Applicant had filed, without giving him notice or an opportunity to respond.

propositions.text: RPD's weighing of evidence is ordinary process; sworn testimony given more weight than unsworn letters.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the RPD engaged in the ordinary process of weighing evidence, and that it was simply giving effect to the well-known legal principle that sworn documentation and live testimony by witnesses will be given more weight than unsworn letters.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed supporting evidence should be given little weight in establishing sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s review of this evidence confirmed that it should be given little weight in establishing the Applicant’s sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant's relationship evidence vague, rejected procedural fairness claim, upheld RPD's evidence weighing, and gave little weight to supporting evidence.

propositions.text: RAD concluded Applicant had not established he is gay or perceived as gay and rejected claim.
propositions.quote: Based on its review of the evidence, the RAD concluded that the Applicant had not established that he is gay or perceived to be gay, and therefore it rejected his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concluded the Applicant failed to establish he is or is perceived as gay and rejected his claim.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD erred by failing to follow SOGIE Guidelines properly.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of this decision, arguing that the RAD erred by: (i) failing to properly follow the SOGIE Guidelines;

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD denied procedural fairness by requiring sworn affidavits and live witnesses.
propositions.quote: (ii) denying the Applicant procedural fairness by requiring sworn affidavits and live witnesses;

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD misapprehended evidence on crucial points.
propositions.quote: (iii) misapprehending the evidence on crucial points.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RAD erred by not following SOGIE Guidelines, denying procedural fairness, and misapprehending evidence.

propositions.text: Standard of review for first and third issues is reasonableness per Huruglica 2016 FCA 93 para 35.
propositions.quote: The standard of review for the first and third issues is reasonableness: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93 at para 35.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness is assessed like correctness but must be fair and reasonable in context per Khosa 2009 SCC 12 para 43 and CPR 2018 FCA 69 para 54.
propositions.quote: The issue of procedural fairness is assessed in a manner which resembles the correctness standard, but in the end a reviewing court must determine whether the process was fair and reasonable in the circumstances: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43; Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness for first and third issues, and procedural fairness is assessed for fairness and reasonableness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review concerns substantive outcome and reasoning process requiring justification, transparency, intelligibility per Igloo Vikski 2016 SCC 38 para 18.
propositions.quote: The key question in a judicial review on the standard of reasonableness is summarized in Canada (Attorney General) v Igloo Vikski Inc, 2016 SCC 38, [2016] 2 SCR 80: [18] Reasonableness review is concerned with the reasonableness of the substantive outcome of the decision, and with the process of articulating that outcome.

propositions.text: Reasoning must show justification, transparency, intelligibility per Dunsmuir 2008 SCC 9 para 47.
propositions.quote: The reasoning must exhibit “justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process”: Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190, at para. 47.

propositions.text: Outcome and reasons must show result within range of possible outcomes per Newfoundland Nurses 2011 SCC 62 para 14.
propositions.quote: The substantive outcome and the reasons, considered together, must serve the purpose of showing whether the result falls within a range of possible outcomes: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v. Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 708, at para. 14.

propositions.text: Adequacy of reasons is not alone a basis for review but reasons should adequately explain decision basis per Newfoundland Nurses para 18 and Canada Post 2010 FCA 56 para 163.
propositions.quote: While the adequacy of a tribunal’s reasons is not on its own a discrete basis for judicial review, the reasons should “adequately explain the bases of [the] decision”: Newfoundland Nurses, at para. 18, quoting from Canada Post Corp. v. Public Service Alliance of Canada, 2010 FCA 56, [2011] 2 F.C.R. 221, at para. 163 (per Evans J.A., dissenting), rev’d 2011 SCC 57, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 572.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness review requires justified, transparent, intelligible reasoning showing the decision falls within possible outcomes.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review focuses on whether decision-maker engaged with evidence applying correct legal test; standard is not perfection.
propositions.quote: To put it another way, in a judicial review on the deferential standard of reasonableness, a key concern is whether the process and decision indicate that the decision-maker truly “engaged” with the evidence, applying the appropriate legal test. The standard is not perfection.

propositions.text: Deference is due to administrative decision-maker especially on factual inquiries within expertise and policy context.
propositions.quote: It must be recalled that Parliament assigned the task of conducting the initial inquiry into the facts to the administrative decision-maker. Deference is due to a decision-maker, especially in a context where the inquiry is primarily factual, the subject-matter is within the decision-maker’s area of expertise, and where greater exposure to the nuances of evidence or a greater awareness of the policy context may provide an advantage.

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness review asks if decision-maker engaged with evidence applying law; deference is due on factual expertise.

propositions.text: If decision-maker's reasoning chain is understandable and shows engagement, decision is generally reasonable per Komolafe 2013 FC 431.
propositions.quote: If the chain of reasoning of the decision-maker can be understood, and if it shows that this type of engagement occurred, the decision will generally be found to be reasonable: see Komolafe v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 431.

propositions.text: Decision-maker need not mention every piece of evidence or step in analysis for reasonableness.
propositions.quote: It is not a reviewable error for the decision-maker to omit reference to every piece of evidence that was considered, or to fail to mention a particular step in the sequence of analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court states understandable reasoning showing engagement is reasonable; omission of some evidence or steps is not error.

propositions.text: Reviewing court cannot ignore or replace reasons actually provided; additional reasons must supplement analysis per Delta Air Lines 2018 SCC 2 para 24.
propositions.quote: A decision cannot be upheld because of what it might or ought to have said, if doing so involves ignoring or discounting the reasoning that was actually expressed in the decision. As Chief Justice McLaughlin (as she then was) said in Delta Air Lines Inc. v Lukács, 2018 SCC 2, [2018] 1 SCR 6 at para 24: “In other words, while a reviewing court may supplement the reasons given in support of an administrative decision, it cannot ignore or replace the reasons actually provided. Additional reasons must supplement and not supplant the analysis of the administrative body.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states a reviewing court cannot ignore or replace the reasons given; additional reasons must supplement, not supplant analysis.

propositions.text: The RAD decision is unreasonable due to focus on microscopic, tangential, or inaccurate evidence statements.
propositions.quote: In this case, I find the decision of the RAD to be unreasonable because of the accumulation of instances in which its reasons focus on microscopic, tangentially relevant or inaccurate statements of the evidence.

propositions.text: There may be reasonable bases to discount testimony and documentation, but RAD's reasons do not rely on these for credibility findings.
propositions.quote: While I find that there may have been reasonable bases to discount the Applicant’s testimony and supporting documentation, the actual reasons expressed by the RAD do not rely on these as a basis for its credibility findings.

propositions.text: The RAD decision is unreasonable and must be sent back for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: The decision is unreasonable and must be sent back for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD decision unreasonable due to flawed reasoning and orders reconsideration.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD failed to follow letter and spirit of SOGIE Guidelines in considering all evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the RAD failed to follow the letter and spirit of the SOGIE Guidelines in its consideration of all of the evidence.

propositions.text: RAD mentioned Guidelines for port of entry credibility but not for other evidence, which is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: It mentions the Guidelines and appears to follow them in its assessment of the credibility of the Applicant’s statements at the port of entry, but not in relation to any of the other evidence. This is not reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues RAD failed to follow SOGIE Guidelines fully; the court finds partial application unreasonable.

propositions.text: Guidelines are not binding but must be applied or explained if not followed.
propositions.quote: The Guidelines are not binding, but they must be applied by decision-makers or an explanation must be given for not following them.

propositions.text: McKenzie v Canada confirms Guidelines must be applied or explained if not followed.
propositions.quote: see the discussion in McKenzie v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 555 at paras 44-46.

propositions.text: RAD cites Guidelines and shows application regarding contradictions in Applicant's port of entry evidence.
propositions.quote: In this case the RAD cites the Guidelines and then demonstrates how it is applying them in the context of its consideration of the ontradictions and difficulties with the Applicant’s evidence at the port of entry.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Guidelines must be applied or explained if not followed, citing McKenzie, and notes RAD applied them to Applicant's port of entry evidence.

propositions.text: It is unclear if RAD considered Guidelines for other evidence, but this alone doesn't justify overturning the decision.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that it is not evident whether or how the RAD considered the Guidelines in its assessment of any of the other evidence. On its own, however, this is not a sufficient basis to overturn the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees it's unclear if RAD considered Guidelines for other evidence but this alone doesn't justify overturning the decision.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD engaged in microscopic analysis to discount credibility or probative value of information.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to a number of instances in which the RAD engaged in a microscopic analysis of a particular detail as its basis to discount the credibility or probative value of the information.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues RAD used microscopic analysis to discount credibility of evidence.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant gave contradictory evidence about schools attended and rejected explanation of stress at port of entry.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the Applicant gave contradictory evidence about the schools he attended, noting that in the student visa application and Basis of Claim form he submitted, the Applicant stated he attended one school while at the port of entry he gave the name of another school.

propositions.text: RAD finds Applicant's first port of entry statement more credible and views later school name changes as fabricated narrative.
propositions.quote: Again, a simple explanation is more credible to me: the [Applicant] was telling the truth when he was first asked about his education at the POE. In my view, the evidence is consistent with a fabricated narrative about the [Applicant’s] sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant gave contradictory school evidence and rejected stress explanation, viewing first statement as truthful and later as fabricated.

propositions.text: Applicant argues refugee narrative does not depend on boarding school attendance and RAD's finding is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that this reasoning is flawed because his refugee narrative is not dependent in any way on his attendance at a boarding school.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues his refugee narrative doesn't depend on boarding school attendance and RAD's contrary finding is unreasonable.

propositions.text: RAD gave little weight to friend's letter as it was belief-based and not from a partner, preferring oral testimony.
propositions.quote: The RAD gave little weight to a letter from the Applicant’s friend in Canada, since it found that the letter “indicates that person’s belief but it does not purport to be from a partner who would have a more reliable view of the [Applicant’s] sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Applicant submits RAD contradicts SOGIE Guidelines by requiring oral testimony over written evidence and not engaging with letter content.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that this finding is in direct contradiction to the SOGIE Guidelines, because the RAD does not demonstrate an understanding that it may be difficult or impossible for a person to obtain evidence from sexual partners, and it is, in effect, requiring oral testimony rather than weighing written evidence in support of a claim.

paragraphs.summary: RAD gave little weight to friend's letter preferring oral testimony; Applicant argues this contradicts SOGIE Guidelines and RAD failed to engage with letter content.

propositions.text: RAD rejected cousin's letter as not credible due to incorrect number of sisters named, implying fabrication.
propositions.quote: I find that this letter is not credible and further impugns the credibility of the [Applicant] because it names and repeatedly refers to his two younger sisters, contradicting the [Applicant’s] BOC, which names three younger sisters from his parents’ marriage, all under the age of 15.

paragraphs.summary: RAD rejected cousin's letter as not credible due to incorrect number of sisters named, implying fabrication.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD's rejection of cousin's letter on sister count is microscopic and ignores letter's content and context.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that this is a microscopic analysis of an irrelevant point. The number of sisters the Applicant has is irrelevant to his complaint.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD's rejection of cousin's letter based on sister count is microscopic and ignores content and context.

propositions.text: RAD gave no weight to uncle's letters due to credibility doubts from alleged false statement on Basis of Claim form.
propositions.quote: the RAD found that the uncle had assisted the Applicant to complete the original Basis of Claim form, and had signed the form indicating that he had interpreted it for the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: RAD gave no weight to uncle's letters due to credibility doubts from alleged false statement on Basis of Claim form.

propositions.text: Applicant argues uncle made mistakes completing form, so RAD's conclusion of fraudulent intent is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to a number of incorrect or inaccurate statements in the original basis of claim form, and suggests that this makes it evident that although the uncle did his best to help the Applicant complete the form, it is obvious that he made a number of mistakes.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues uncle made mistakes completing form, so RAD's conclusion of fraudulent intent is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant points out RAD failed to refer to mother's letter despite her personal knowledge of key events.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points out that the RAD failed to refer to the letter from the Applicant’s mother, despite her personal knowledge of the key events that led him to flee Ghana and claim refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant notes RAD failed to refer to mother's letter despite her personal knowledge of key events.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD breached procedural fairness by not addressing submission about RPD ignoring key evidence and not advising concerns.
propositions.quote: Finally, the Applicant argues that the RAD breached procedural fairness when it failed to meaningfully address its submission that the RPD failed to consider the key evidence in the letters because they were not sworn and without advising the Applicant of its concerns.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD breached procedural fairness by not addressing submission about RPD ignoring key evidence and not advising concerns.

propositions.text: Respondent contends RAD reasonably found RPD did not err applying general rules preferring sworn evidence and oral testimony.
propositions.quote: The Respondent contends that the RAD reasonably found that the RPD did not err in applying the general rules of evidence, preferring sworn evidence to unsworn letters, and oral testimony to written documentation.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent contends RAD reasonably found RPD did not err applying general rules preferring sworn evidence and oral testimony.

propositions.text: Respondent submits RAD's credibility assessment deserves deference and was supported by contradictions and omissions in Applicant's narrative.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the decision and outcome must be viewed as an organic whole, and that the RAD’s assessment of credibility is owed significant deference.

propositions.text: Respondent notes contradictions about relationship length and partner information undermined Applicant's credibility.
propositions.quote: The Applicant gave contradictory evidence about the length of his first relationship, and failed to provide basic information about his second partner.

propositions.text: Respondent argues RAD did not err in finding omissions and contradictions affected Applicant's credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not err in finding that these omissions and contradictions about the core of the claim affected the Applicant’s credibility: Ogaulu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 547 at para 20.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits RAD's credibility assessment deserves deference, supported by contradictions and omissions in Applicant's narrative.

propositions.text: Respondent argues discrepancies about school attended were material and undermined Applicant's credibility.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Respondent argues that the discrepancies in the Applicant’s evidence about which school he attended were material.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues discrepancies about school attended were material and undermined Applicant's credibility.

propositions.text: Respondent argues RAD reasonably considered documentary evidence credibility in light of Applicant's credibility findings.
propositions.quote: It was both reasonable and appropriate for the RAD to consider the credibility and reliability of the documentary evidence in light of its earlier findings about the Applicant’s credibility, and the decision makes clear that the RAD carefully considered the evidence in its totality.

propositions.text: It is not the Court's role to re-weigh evidence.
propositions.quote: It is not the role of the Court to re-weigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RAD reasonably considered documentary evidence credibility; court states it is not role to re-weigh evidence.

propositions.text: Court agrees RAD's decision is not reasonable due to microscopic analysis without merit weighing.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that the RAD’s decision is not reasonable, because several significant evidentiary findings were based on a microscopic analysis of particular, specific aspects of the evidence, and there is no indication that the RAD engaged in any analysis or weighing of the evidence on its merits.

propositions.text: Supreme Court says court must not ignore or replace RAD's own explanation of findings.
propositions.quote: To recall the words of the Supreme Court, it is not the role of the Court to ignore or replace the words the RAD actually used to explain its findings.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees RAD's decision is unreasonable due to microscopic analysis without merit weighing, recalling Supreme Court guidance.

propositions.text: RAD discounted cousin's letter solely on sister count, ignoring substance and context, which is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD mentions that the cousin’s letter outlines his suspicions about the Applicant’s sexual orientation and recounts what he was told by the Applicant’s mother, but these are not referred to as the basis for the RAD’s conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD discounted cousin's letter solely on sister count, ignoring substance and context, unreasonably.

propositions.text: RAD analyzed uncle's letter by focusing on one form contradiction without considering letter substance or context.
propositions.quote: The RAD seizes on a prior basis of claim form that the Applicant completed with the assistance of the uncle, notes that he contradicted the statement on that form that it had been translated to him, and then concludes that this called into question the uncle’s credibility to such an extent that the letter was given no weight.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD analyzed uncle's letter focusing on one contradiction without considering substance or context.

propositions.text: Court agrees omissions and contradictions raise credibility questions but RAD must consider all evidence reasonably.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent’s argument that there are significant omissions and contradictions in the Applicant’s evidence, which could raise legitimate questions about his credibility.

propositions.text: RAD failed to analyze and consider evidence reasonably on its merits, falling short on key fronts.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s decision falls short on several key fronts in this regard, as demonstrated above.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees credibility issues exist but RAD failed to reasonably analyze and consider evidence on merits.

propositions.text: Judicial review of a RAD decision is a deferential reasonableness review, not a line-by-line error search.
propositions.quote: Judicial review of a RAD decision should not be a line-by-line treasure hunt for error, but rather the court is required to examine the reasons and outcome to determine whether they demonstrate that the result falls within the range of reasonable outcomes.

propositions.text: Parliament assigned evidence review to RPD and RAD; court must not usurp that role.
propositions.quote: Parliament has assigned the task of reviewing and assessing the evidence to the RPD and then the RAD. It is not the role of this Court to usurp that role.

propositions.text: The standard of review is reasonableness, not perfection.
propositions.quote: The standard is not perfection, but rather reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that judicial review of RAD decisions is deferential, focusing on reasonableness, not perfection or error hunting, respecting Parliament's role.

propositions.text: The evidentiary record could support the RAD's conclusion on the claim's merits.
propositions.quote: there was much in the evidentiary record that could have supported the RAD’s conclusion on the merits of the claim.

propositions.text: However, the RAD's explanation at key points cannot be ignored and is problematic.
propositions.quote: I find that at several key points in its analysis the RAD’s explanation for its reasoning simply cannot be ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the evidence could support RAD's conclusion but its reasoning at key points is problematic and cannot be ignored.

propositions.text: It is unclear if RAD applied SOGIE Guidelines to all evidence.
propositions.quote: It is not clear whether the RAD applied the SOGIE Guidelines to its consideration of all of the evidence.

propositions.text: RAD's credibility doubts focus on minor details, not substance or context of evidence.
propositions.quote: its explanation for questioning the credibility of the Applicant, his cousin and his uncle are explained with reference to microscopic analysis of tangential details rather than the substance or overall context for the evidence.

propositions.text: The Applicant’s mother's letter, providing direct evidence, is not mentioned by RAD.
propositions.quote: The letter from the Applicant’s mother, which provides more direct evidence, is not mentioned.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD unclear on applying SOGIE Guidelines, focusing on minor details over substance, and ignoring key evidence like the mother's letter.

propositions.text: The RAD's reasoning relies on irrelevant or minor details without analyzing evidence substance or context.
propositions.quote: it appears that it has based key determinations on largely irrelevant or minor points of detail, without any analysis of the substance of the evidence or the context within which it was given.

propositions.text: The court can follow RAD's reasoning chain but finds it flawed at key points.
propositions.quote: I can follow the chain of reasoning of the RAD, at several key points it appears that it has based key determinations on largely irrelevant or minor points of detail

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD's reasoning flawed by relying on minor irrelevant details without substantive or contextual analysis, though the reasoning chain is traceable.

propositions.text: Decision-making must show justification, transparency, and intelligibility as required by Dunsmuir and Jakutavicius.
propositions.quote: The reasoning does not demonstrate “justification, transparency and intelligibility” within the decision-making process, as required by Dunsmuir (and see the discussion in Jakutavicius v Canada (Attorney General), 2011 FC 311 at para 31).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RAD's reasoning lacks required justification, transparency, and intelligibility per Dunsmuir and Jakutavicius.

propositions.text: The RAD decision is unreasonable for reasons explained above.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out above, I find the decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: No need to address procedural fairness argument due to unreasonableness conclusion.
propositions.quote: In light of my conclusion on this issue, it is not necessary to address the procedural fairness argument in any detail.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD decision is unreasonable and declines to address procedural fairness arguments.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is granted, RAD decision overturned, and matter remitted to a different RAD panel.
propositions.quote: I am therefore granting the application for judicial review. The RAD decision is overturned and the matter is sent back for reconsideration by a different panel of the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, overturns the RAD decision, and remits the matter to a different RAD panel.

propositions.text: Judgment allows judicial review, overturns RAD decision, remits matter to different RAD panel, and denies certification.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The decision of the Refugee Appeal Division is overturned. The matter is sent back for reconsideration by a different panel of the Refugee Appeal Division. There is no question of general importance for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders judicial review allowed, RAD decision overturned, matter remitted, and denies certification for a question of general importance.
